title: Clinical Skills
tagline: Communication, history taking, physical examination, clinical reasoning and interpreting tests
summary: Diagnosis starts with talking to and examining the patient. This course covers communication and history taking, physical examination, clinical reasoning, the interpretation of laboratory tests and medical imaging, records and handover, and patient safety.
overview: Medicine is practised through conversations, examinations, test results and notes. The history usually suggests the diagnosis, the examination tests it, and investigations confirm or refute it. When care goes wrong, the cause is often a failure of communication or of a system rather than a gap in scientific knowledge. This course treats the core clinical skills as subjects that can be taught, practised and assessed like any basic science.

It begins with communication: the structure of the consultation, listening and explaining, shared decisions, talking about risk and difficult conversations. It then covers the medical history and the physical examination, including vital signs and NEWS2, the main body systems and the accuracy of physical signs. The chapter on clinical reasoning explains how hypotheses are generated and tested, how Bayes' theorem and likelihood ratios underlie every test request, and how cognitive biases lead to diagnostic error. Two chapters then show how to choose and interpret laboratory tests, blood gases and imaging.

The final chapters cover the infrastructure of safe care: good records, medicines reconciliation, structured handover and escalation, and teamwork; and patient safety, including human factors, the Swiss cheese model, checklists, incident reporting, a just culture, the duty of candour and quality improvement. Every chapter has worked clinical examples, common pitfalls, quick checks and exercises with full answers. The content follows UK practice and guidance (NICE, the Royal College of Physicians, the GMC and NHS England) and notes where international guidance applies; it is educational and not a substitute for local guidelines.
outcomes: Structure a consultation using the Calgary–Cambridge guide, explore the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations, explain using chunk-and-check and teach-back, and break bad news using SPIKES.
Take and present a complete or focused medical history, including a drug history with allergies, pack-years, alcohol units and presentation-specific red flags.
Perform a systematic examination of the main body systems, calculate NEWS2 and the GCS, and interpret the classic signs while stating what each sign can and cannot exclude.
Apply Bayes' theorem with likelihood ratios, test and treatment thresholds and clinical prediction rules such as the Wells score, and recognise the cognitive biases that cause diagnostic error.
Interpret reference intervals, predictive values and common blood tests, recognise pre-analytical errors, and read an arterial blood gas including compensation and the anion gap.
Explain how X-ray, CT, ultrasound, MRI and nuclear medicine work, read a chest X-ray systematically, and weigh radiation dose, contrast risks and MRI safety when choosing a test.
Write problem-based records, reconcile medicines, hand over using SBAR and I-PASS, and communicate effectively in a clinical team.
Describe the human-factors view of error, distinguish strong from weak safety interventions, and outline incident reporting, just culture, the duty of candour and PDSA-based quality improvement.

history.title: The bedside as method
history.detail: The Hippocratic writings put observation and the recorded case at the centre of medicine. The Epidemics describe individual patients day by day, and other texts advise on the physician's conduct and speech at the bedside.

history.title: Percussion
history.detail: Leopold Auenbrugger publishes Inventum Novum, describing percussion of the chest to detect fluid and solid lung. The method is ignored until Corvisart promotes it in Paris around 1808.

history.title: The stethoscope
history.detail: René Laennec rolls paper into a tube to listen to a patient's heart, develops the wooden monaural stethoscope, and in 1819 publishes De l'auscultation médiate, relating sounds heard in life to findings after death.

history.title: Hand hygiene
history.detail: In Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis shows that maternal deaths from puerperal fever fall sharply when doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime before examining women in labour.

history.title: X-rays
history.detail: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovers X-rays in Würzburg; within weeks radiographs are being used in medicine, beginning the age of imaging.

history.title: The doctor as a drug
history.detail: Michael Balint's book The Doctor, His Patient and the Illness, based on seminars with London general practitioners, argues that the doctor's own behaviour acts like a drug, and makes the consultation itself a subject of study.

history.title: The problem-oriented record
history.detail: Lawrence Weed publishes 'Medical records that guide and teach' in the New England Journal of Medicine, introducing the problem list and the structured progress note that became the SOAP format.

history.title: Computed tomography
history.detail: The first clinical CT scan of a patient's head is performed in London on a scanner built by Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; he shares the 1979 Nobel Prize with Allan Cormack.

history.title: To Err Is Human
history.detail: The US Institute of Medicine report reviews the evidence on preventable adverse events in hospitals and argues that most errors arise from faulty systems rather than reckless individuals, launching the modern patient-safety movement.

history.title: The Surgical Safety Checklist
history.detail: The World Health Organization launches its Surgical Safety Checklist. In a before-and-after study across eight hospitals, published in 2009, deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and complications from 11.0% to 7.0%.
